s1: [warmly] Right now, your body is making millions of new cells, to help you grow and to repair any damage.
s2: [curious] It makes them by mitosis: one cell dividing into two identical cells.
s3: [conspiratorially] But here's the bit people get wrong. [emphatically] The cell copies its DNA before mitosis even starts.
s4: [thoughtfully] Each chromosome becomes two identical copies, joined in the middle.
s5: [building anticipation] Then mitosis begins. The chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell.
s6: [excited] Fibres pull the copies apart, one to each end, and the nucleus divides.
s7: [satisfied] Finally the cytoplasm and cell membrane split, and there are two new cells, each with exactly the same chromosomes as the first.
q: [playfully] Quick check. [curious] Does the cell copy its DNA before mitosis, or during it?
a: [warmly, pleased] Before. That's why both new cells get a full set.
